newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Nemtsov is golden boy of economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Nemtsov is golden boy of economic reform.

text.p: Boris Nemtsov, the 37-year-old regional governor who was appointed first deputy prime minister on Monday, is the "golden boy" of Russia's market reforms and a potential presidential candidate for the year 2000.

President Boris Yeltsin has long viewed Nemtsov as a potential successor. His boyish good looks, mop of dark curly hair and easy television manner in both Russian and English have made him a household name far beyond his fiefdom of Nizhny Novgorod.
"You can already tip him for president," Yeltsin said of Nemtsov as long as three years ago.

Nemtsov returned the compliment by throwing his support behind Yeltsin's reelection last year, turning down earnest entreaties from his squabbling fellow-liberals to unite their camp and run against the now 66-year-old president.
Nemtsov, perhaps best remembered in the West for flinging a glass of juice over ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky on live television, joined Yeltsin's campaign team.
The campaign was run by fellow reformer, 41-year-old Anatoly Chubais, with whom Nemtsov will share the rank of first deputy premier in the new government being formed this week.
Though he has never held a cabinet post before, Nemtsov's name has come up regularly in the media over the past few years as a potential successor to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

But on Monday he said his new job may damage his future political chances since he will have to make unpopular decisions. "I've written off my political future," he told reporters in Nizhny Novgorod, Interfax news agency reported.
His career is closely associated with the ancient Russian city of Nizhny Novgorod on the Volga river, 400 km (250 miles) east of Moscow.
For most of the Soviet era it was renamed Gorky after the writer Maxim Gorky and closed to foreigners. Dissident Andrei Sakharov was confined there in internal exile.
Under Nemtsov, the carmaking city and surrounding region pioneered privatisation and other market reforms and is seen by many Western experts as a model for the rest of Russia.

The reform programme was drawn up by liberal economist and Yabloko party leader Grigory Yavlinsky, with whom Nemtsov collaborated closely. They have since parted ways, apparently to some extent because of Yavlinsky's bitter antagonism to Yeltsin.
For all his youth, Nemtsov has shown himself a tough politician, standing up to local and national criticism of his radical policies.
When Zhirinovsky called him a "scumbag" and threw orange juice at him during a television debate in 1995, Nemtsov had no hesitation in replying in kind.
An opinion poll last December made him Russia's fourth most-trusted politician after law-and-order advocate General Alexander Lebed, Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov and Yavlinsky.

Born in the Black Sea resort of Sochi, Nemtsov graduated in radio physics from Gorky University in 1981 and worked as an engineer in the city. He took his first steps in politics during the Soviet era as an environmental campaigner.
In 1990, at the age of 30, he was elected a deputy to the Russian Federation Supreme Soviet and then moved on to the Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union.
Yeltsin appointed him head of the Nizhny Novgorod administration in November 1991 as the Soviet Union broke up, giving Nemtsov a seat in the Federation Council upper house.
He was elected in December 1995 and returned, comfortably, last autumn.
Nemtsov made a media splash when Nizhny Novgorod region was the first in Russia to auction off small shops and firms, and to sell municipally-owned trucking operations to drivers.

In 1993, launching a pilot project with a unit of the World Bank, a state farm near Nizhny Novgorod made history as the first in Russia to go private since Stalin's brutal collectivisation drive in the 1930s.
Nemtsov, like Yeltsin before his recent heart trouble, is a keen tennis player. He is married and has one daughter.
